newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels reject ceasefire pressure, summit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels reject ceasefire pressure, summit.

text.p: Zairean rebels on Wednesday shrugged off mounting international pressure for a ceasefire and said a meeting of African leaders that excluded rebel representatives would not solve anything.

"What counts for us is our people. Although we cannot ignore outside pressure, our people need this war to finish quickly and do not want a ceasefire," rebel information commissioner Raphael Nghenda told Reuters.

A one-day meeting chaired by Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi opened in Nairobi on Wednesday with the presidents of Zimbabwe and Congo, South Africa's deputy president, Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and representatives of Cameroon.
South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo told Reuters before the talks that South Africa hoped for a ceasefire as the foundation of a political settlement.
The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) has seized a fifth of Zaire since launching its rebellion in October to overthrow ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
European Union special envoy Aldo Ajello, attending the meeting as an observer, also called for a ceasefire. The United States and France appealed jointly for a ceasefire on Tuesday.
"The Nairobi summit could only have a very doubtful impact without our presence, and it is clearly not going to produce a serious result when Moi is such a close ally of Mobutu," said Nghenda.
Kenya's government says the rebels were not invited because they are not a government. Zaire attended Wednesday's talks after boycotting two previous Nairobi meetings on the problem.
On Saturday the rebels took the eastern city of Kisangani, their biggest prize so far and the base in January for a failed government counter-offensive backed by foreign mercenaries.
With its forces advancing, the AFDL rules out any ceasefire before negotiations and says talks can only be held directly with Mobutu, or somebody appointed by him, to discuss a handover of power.
"Essentially we want frank and sincere discussions and we are willing to sit down at the table with those who hold power at any time, as we have always said," Nghenda said in Goma city.

The rebels say they are moving closer to Mbuji-Mayi, diamond mining capital of the central Kasai region, and south into Shaba region, with some of the world's richest unexploited reserves of copper and cobalt.

"We need to reach Mbuji-Mayi quickly so soldiers and mercenaries who fled there do not have time to destroy the mining installations and steal all they can from the people before retreating," said Nghenda.
The city of Mbuji-Mayi is the home base of Zaire's richest company, MIBA, which mines largely industrial diamonds.
Rebel Voice of the People radio on Wednesday warned Zairean army officers to lay down their weapons before the arrival of advancing rebels or face charges of treason.
Broadcasting from the eastern city of Goma, it said the officers would be charged with "high treason and rebellion against the legitimate authority" of the AFDL, which is led by Laurent Kabila.
It said officers should leave their weapons at Zaire's second largest city of Lubumbashi in Shaba or at Kikwit, 500 km (300 miles) east of the capital Kinshasa, before the rebels arrived.
